newsitem.title: USA: Democratic candidates in election more moderate.
newsitem.headline: Democratic candidates in election more moderate.

text.p: If Democrats win control of the House of Representatives in November it will be with the help of victorious candidates who believe President Bill Clinton's declaration that the era of big government is over.
Republicans charge that, if Democrats win, "liberals" are poised to grab control of powerful House committees and move full speed ahead to raise taxes and boost government spending.
But even some Democrats said the power of liberal committee chairmen would be diluted by a new wave of moderate Democratic members of Congress.

Analysts say the Democrats have a decent shot at making the net gains necessary to regain a majority in the 435-seat House, where Republicans have a 235-198 edge with one seat vacant and one independent who votes with the Democrats.
Control of the House means the party in power can set the legislative agenda and use the committee structure to put its favourite issues in the spotlight.

Republicans dismiss Democratic chances of reversing the 1994 outcome, which brought Republicans to power in the House for the first time in 40 years. But with many races in doubt, Republicans are sounding an alarm about what Democrats would do if they do take over.
"Their true agenda is a liberal agenda, marked by greater government control, more spending and higher taxes," declared Republican National Committee Chairman Haley Barbour.

He pointed to members such as Wisconsin Democrat David Obey, first in line to chair the powerful Appropriations Committee, which controls most spending. Obey wants government to expand its reach rather than contract.
But the new breed of Democratic candidates include many fiscal conservatives for whom balancing the federal budget is an article of faith.

Some voted for a welfare reform plan Clinton signed into law over the objections of liberals such as Democratic Representative Anthony Beilenson of California, who complained it would hurt the poor. Beilenson is retiring and the Democrat running to replace him, Brad Sherman, feels differently.
"I probably would have cast a vote in favour," says Sherman, despite his belief the welfare measure needed some changes.

Even in the inner cities things are changing. Julia Carson, running to replace retiring Democratic Representative Andrew Jacobs in Indianapolis, opposed the welfare bill but ran a tough welfare system herself in that Midwest city.
Carson, who was on welfare as a child, cut 85,000 people from the rolls, instituted "workfare" requiring people to earn their benefits and slashed $9.3 million.

And in the Washington state primary this month, moderate Democrats beat liberals in three districts to face conservative first-term Republicans. During a visit last week, Clinton said Washington has "a bigger opportunity than any other state to say 'we need change in Congress.'"

These new Democrats, running for open seats or challenging Republicans, are modelling themselves on Clinton, who once proposed a major expansion of government power in health care but now says he is not a liberal.
"We will have an infusion of moderate Democrats who want to win re-election as well as election," said Democratic Representative Howard Berman of California.
